The price of a meriiher's vote ranged, artier George 111., from rat) to ilariak Mr. Grenville, in asking Lord Saye and Sole, by letter, for his support, enclosed a £2OO itote. Lord Saye wrote back, promising his vote, but retuthing the money. The tonedf Lord Saye's letter in ixtremely courteous, with ahoolutely nothing in it of offended dignity. He merely observes that he has made it a rule never to accept presents of that sort. Mr. Grenville replies by complimenting hilli OD ilk like sense of honour. It was in that reign that Sir Jolui Trevor, Speaker of the House of Commons, wan found guilty of Liking a bribe of a thousand guineas to forward a private Bill. He was ordered to move a vote of censui eon himself front the chair. Next day he was to have moveg his own expolsion front the House. He con- trived, howmer, to be ill on the morrow 1 and the House gombnaturedly accepted the excuse. The Council of the Royal Geographical Society have awarded their gold medals for the present year to Lie.. A. L. Falender, of the Swedish Navy, for his services to geographical science as commander of the Vega in the Swedish Arctic Expedition of 1878-9, and to Me. Ernest Giles for leading various expeditions M Australia, and making valuable route surveys, as well or scientific collec- tions. A gold watch was also awarded to Bishop Crowther for his Rervices to geography during his numerous journeys in the Niger region in the past forty years, and for the addi- tions he has made to our knowledge of the country and the language and customs of the people. The Mus,Se de Cluny has acquired, so says the Chroniyrte ' are Art g, two noteworthy relics, a magnificent procesaional cross of silver gilt of the fourteenth century and a Venetian cabinet of the sixteenth century. The former is adorned with figures in high relief and of fine execution. en one aide are the effigies of Christ, the Virgin, SS. John, Peter, and More Magdalen ; on the other side are the Evangelists with their attributes. The bottom of the cross is ornamented with translucid enamels representing the Apostles and em- blems of the Virtues. This relic is it perfect order and was Cooed in an Apennine convent. It is one of the finest works of its kind, a most desirable addition to the great museum. The price paid by M. du Sommerard was 9,800 francs. Prince Ilemicluff gave 15,000 francs for it. The Cabinet cost the Mus6e 4,500 francs.

, BILL'S TUAY2ConLute AND Ita-a-ranran.—An oven- : tion, having for its object the amistance of horses in stop- I ping anti re-starting tram-cars was tried recently on the trantway line in the Blackfriara-road, London, under the auspices of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. The invention is that of Mr. W. Bell, of , Bishomptte-street Within, and it consists of a system of , coiled springs, levers, and gearing, nlaced at the end of each I one under the framing. The springs are connected, by means of a crosshead and chain, with a loom drum and clutch gearing working on the axle on which the train-car wheels are fixed. When thy signal is given to the driver to stop the on, he releasm a lever, which throws a fixed clutch into gearing with the loose drum to which the chain is attached. The drum then revolves with the axle of the one and whit's up the chain, thus causing retarding force to he exerted on the wheels by reason of the springs becoming compressed. On receiving the signal to go on, the driver releaaes the clutch from the drum, and the springs, now having free play, unwind the chain from off the drum. In no doing, the drum—and with it the axle of the car—is re- volved in a forward direction, which gives an inipetus to the car, thus assisting the horses at the start. The efficiency of the invention as a brake was satisfactorily proved with the horses in, the car being pulled op within remarkably -hort distances. To tmt its value as an auxiliary in starting a car, the horse, were removed and the vehicle was propelled forwards to a considerable distance by the aid of the springs alone, thus demonstrating the mei it of the invention in thia respect.— Times.

The other evening Mr. J. Chalmers Morton rea I be- fore the Society of Arts a paper entitled "Agricultural Experience; the Lemons of Forty Ymrs."—Mr. J.. Caird prmitled.—Mr. Mout.oet explained in detail a Reeks of eLtho- rate coloured dimgranss illustrating, from 1840 to 1870 in- clusive, the composition of English soils, the character and duration of harvests, the average price of grain, and the' receipts, with their respective sources, from a number of farms and estates in different paats of the country. These diagrams, he mid, showed the fickle claracter vf farm ex- not me might ahnost say that there was little in , them to suggess—harilly anything to justify—rules of con- ' duct. One of the tirincipal Immt. taught by them was, he submitted, the need of leaving such a fickle and uhcertain business as for as possible unfettered by melt rules, no that the master, able to one hi, opportunities led educated by his experience, should be the more capable of dmling with his iithoroltirnoo they unexpectedly .me. The diagrams indi- cated that the q.ntitien of moat., whether from corn- fields, herd,, or dock.% were increasing year by year, though no doubt the curve of increasing population ruse even faster and more regularly. It, mid nothing of iocreasing emt, the, MIS at any rate no sign there of the allegro! decadence of English agriculture to for Co it. produce WM concereed. Another lesson taught by the diagram was pa- tience ; they showed that a long iwrital of disastex had heen no extraortli.ry experience in the history of English agriculture, which had nevertheless survived and again at- tained prosperity. 'The MAill 1c0n,,, however, taught by the last of English agriculture, as there depicted, was the para. mount necessity of liberty of action for those who followed it ea their occupation. The diagram representing the rain- fall was a perfect jig, but it was the tune that the farmera had Co dance to, and only them who were unencumbered , could keep time to it. The miserable expahent, after me- cemive bad season, of remitting 20, 30, and 50 per cent- of the , year's rent might be the best thing that could Le dole in the , ineantime. But what was the likeliest mitignion in the long ' run, what th eI i keliestsou rce of strength the f uture? If they saw my of their own teams almmt beaten as they strum,,,led up any hill of difficulty, they would explain, Loosen all tine, Marieo reim and trammels which hamper and restrain Mein. Give them their heads, and there will ire. for than." Ilut tenant farmers, mo .0 rule, in England had not had their Imola allow.' them. To tM or man down by rules of cultivation, to make o...custom of the country" It,, perpetual master, and then to set hint to contend with seasons, doals, drough., blights, disease, and, worse than all, with competition in his market with imports sent by cultivaton, who were unbound and free—this sr. to leave him without A chance. Landlord. should Mrive to have mmtey-making temente, and tenant. should have liberty to inake their (monies off the land if possible. Lind which yielded fortune to its tellantS Wint ceruin to yield rent to its owners. Lord Leieester gave absolute liberty over hi, large estates, and he had not as yet seen any reason to regret the course he adopted nine years ago. The lesson of forty years of agrii•uli oral experience was, that liberty and education were the heeds of English agriculture, and the only true bases of ultimate prosperity. He comended that, while landlord and tmant were one, the tenant was that one; that the central figure of English agriculture was the tenant farmer ; and that upon his power, independence, md capacity depended the intereats of landlord, tenant, and labourer alike.—Mr. MECH. made tome remarks, in which he condemn,' ore, natimalmistake the washing of new,ge, by the Areing of which there would be lees necessity for the importation el foal, while the money spent on guano would he kept ill the country.—Mr. C. S. Exao agreed that tenants ought to have liberty, as advocated by Mr. Morton. He expressed mute surprise at the statements that the produce of land had increase', and he thought this must be ac- counted for by tile sales of matt. Ile regrettal that in the present ntate of meteorological seimce the weather could not be predicted with any degree of certainty.— Mr. DENT said that good weather seer, after all, what the tenant most wanted. He was inclined to hope that the womt of the agricultural deprmsion was passed. Ile thought that a tenant', capital should be employes' in working a 'farm, and that the landlord should make the per- manent improvements, wok as drainage; and, speaking ant landlord, he would rather in times of depression expend more money in thme improvements than return to the tenant a part of the rent, though such remissione marked very pleasantly the feeling which existed between landlords and tenants.—Mr. J. llowenn, M.P., said he trusted that the outcome et the agricultural depremion might bet policy of attaching emit:it to the cultivation of the soil, instead of repelling it, and an improvement not only in the LAWS, but the names of the country. One of his most profitable crops was to grow hirley after wheat, but the cultivators over the greater part of England were not at liberty to do to. He consider.' that liberty of cultivation and security for tenants' amital were both raiuired.—Mr. P.m, M.P., said he did not find that there was now touch incream of pro- duce, if any, over, twenty years ago, except where land was then badly cultivated, which was often the case. The value of liberty of action was shown in. case referred to by Mr. Morton, where a farmer, finding that cheese Wile lOW In the market, turned his attention to the supply of milk. In this direction there was an opportunity for farmers, as the con- sumptioa of milk w. insignificant at present, and people bought milk by the teaspoonful when they ought to buy it by the pint. —The CHAIRMAN, in concluding the discussion, said he could not agree with Mr. Dent that the worst was over. A large crop of wheal was expected in America, where there was this year 15 percent. His deduction was that if legislation could do any- thing to take shackles from the landowner and emcee. jest mcurity to the tenant for his capital, the time had come when midething should be done. Unlms every trammel that could be removed was taken off both, the English farmer Gould not stand up against the competition which he now hid to meet.—Mr. MORTON having replied, the meeting broke up.

HOW TO MAKE CHESHIRE CHEESE. We have on various occasions called attention to the valuable article, ;ippearing in Dairy Farming," by Prof. Sheldon, now publishing in monthly numbers by Messrs. Cassell anti CO. It has now reached part 11, and a large mass of interesting anti important preliminary information has been giren. Itt this number" Cheese.inaking " specially treated on, and we publish extracts of the mode of making Cheshire cheese which appear. Our farmer friends will find valuable hints scattered about, which they can appropriate in their present circurnstance.s, and some of which are great labour savers. The article says : Many hundreds of years ago Cheshire cheese had obtained a reputation which was barely approached by that of the cheese of any other county in the kingdom; and in modern i [hoes ts fame has spread to many lands, in some of which imitations of it have beenand are still being made. Cheshire cheese is also made in the adjoining count ire, more particu- larly in Shropshire and Staffordshire, where the same geo- logical formation prevails. There can be no doubt that the properties peculiar to Cheshire Omega, whether it is made in that or in the adjoining countim, are in a great measure owing to the new red sandstone, and to the boulder clay by which it is ucompanied, from which the roil of that part of the country has been derived in the course of ages. Cheshire is also famous on account of its salt deposit,; no doubt the italine element counts for something in the agricultural pro- ducts of the country. It is sufficiently dear that the soil contains some property or properties which influence the character of the herbage, and that the herbage gives to tne milk produced from it, and to the cheese that is made from the milk, certain features that can only in part Le imitated in other districte and countries. It is beyond the need of argument that 11 fine old Chmhire is a mint-11'6cent lump of excellent food. Of late years, however, Cheshire cheese has lost some of its old and excellent reputation. Whether this is owing to the general use of crushed bones and other fer- tilisers on the dairy pastures of the county, whether the Cheshire dairymaids have lost their ancient cunning, or whether too touch skimming of the milk for butter is done, we know cot; Lot it is the universally-received opinion that the cheese of the county, long famnus for its meatinessd quality, flavour, firm...Nand site, is al a rule less excellent than it used to be. It is seldom in the Cheshire system that the cheese is made oftener then once a day, and that once in the morning.
- - finally taken from the oven they are placed in the lever- prtas, providing there is a vacancy for then,, hut as it some- times ham.. that those large cheesed have to remain in

preee w'S4, or even longer, thoee coming out of the oven have to wait their turn to go into press, ualess ample press- room is provided to meet all contingencies. During the ti:ne the cheeses are in preen they are daily turned and dry-clothed, and when finally taken out of press are scald,rl with hot neuter; after the scalding they are gemmed all over to pre, not cracking of the skin, and they are neat swathed in steut hinclagks to preserve them in shape during the subsequent drying. Lastly, they are taken upstairs to the cheese-room, or dryingeoem, where they are turned over at intervals until they are sold to go away. In some of the more advanced dairies there is a handy little lift, by who.. help the chemes are raised by a rope and pulley to the chamber above, thus doing away with the labour of carrying them up the stairs. The lift consists simply of a light framework of wood, which slides up and down between uprights, and the pulley is overhead, in the mom above. The drying-room, or cheese-room, as it is mod generally 0311,01, is commonly the one immediately ever the kitchen or general living-room of the farmer's household, in which case it obtains a good deal of the necessary warmth from below, and this means the Raving of coal above. Many farmem hive hot-water pipes laid round by the wall on the door of the eheese-nairo„ind when properly laid they are on the whole the best inmost( warming the room. Othdre,, again—and these are the most numernue—bsve only a stove in the cheese-room, and though this is a ocelot heat pro- &leer ill, objectionable, on the ground of unequal distribu- tion of the heat produced. The time required to ripen Cheshire cheese varies with the method id making and with the season of the year, generally from two to four month,. It does not nesesaarily follow that the bigger the cheese the longer it will be in 1 ripening; this depends MI the method of making. Yet it j may be stated that, on the onlinary tom-house system of making, the larger cheese will be the longer in ripening at the same time, however, it is true that when the curd is properly warmed and acidified, the cheese made from it will ripen as quickly o'O much smaller one that hon twen made without such manipulation. And in many come, particu- larly where the curd is placed in an oven for a time, the ripening of the large Cheshire cheeses is promoted with a like result, though in it different manner to that which is at once the ornament and strength of the famous Cheddar methal. It cannot be too strongly urged on the notice of cheese-makers that a proper degree of warmth ieoe essential to the ripening of cheese men the ripening of fruit, and that the warmth should be judiciously applied from the time I when the curd is precipitated from the milk until the cheese trendy for the market. Some farmers have a light wooden trough, down which they slide the chem.en from the ebeese-room, through the window, down into the waggon outaide, when they are sent to market. This, too, like the we have spikee of, is a simple and useful device for saving labour. Apart froin the consideration that these large cheeses are awkward things to carry, and are beyond the strength of most dairy- maids, they cannot be carried about by hand without the risk of damaging them, especially when they are fresh from • the prem. It follows, therefore, that the labuur-mv Mg de- vice, we have mentioned, includirig alike the self-turning cheese-ehelves, the lifte, and the slides through the window, can he strongly recomniended ; they to,, as a matter of course, the more valuable in the larger clAirieS and in the factories, but even in smaller dairies of twenty cows or to, they will be found very useful economisers of both Dine and trouble.

In the instance in view the plaintiff demanded l per cent, on an outlay of £16,000, atd the jury awarded .£7o.—Atheneum. Anyhow, do not let the loveliest relic in the isLind be ruined. —Atheneum.

BISHOP FRASER ON TER FUTCRE OF THE C/SYRCTL Preaching at the opening of a new church at Bearnley, on Saturday, the Bishop of Mmchester, in the course of his sermon, said the Church of England embraced all political parties and he hoped they had minds large enough not to allow political opinions to interfere with their religious opinions to interfere with their religious character.Folttical parties needed genial oil to be poured on their controversies, for Oise found often after elections had pawed over bitter feelings had been created, when relatives and relations were sundered by reason of their political differences. The Church of England was not the true church, but a sham and imposter, if she did not do something to mitigate these differences, and bring people together after the strife was over, and to remind them that they were brothers and En- 1 glishmen. He did not know what the future of the Church ' 'of England would be, nor diet be suppose any person else I knew. Great events often came suddenly upon US, Ile was , content to leave future of the Church of England in the I hands of tied, believing that the spirit of Hod is to be counted something amongst the nations of the world, and that there is a drift iu influence, which often great states. ! men, when even at the head of large majorities cannot I afford to despise. If the Church was doing her duty as a I national Church amongst the people committed to her , charge, be thought it would be a very hard thing of any 1 statesman, however advanced, to attempt to disestablish or disendow her. That there may be changes introduced was I possible, and some things necessary he would be glad to see, He did not want the Church hi be charged with maintain- , leg abuses, and be should be the last to wish the Church of England to be maintained merely for the benefit of the clergy. The clergy did not make up the Church of England. There were only 20,000 clergym,n. but there were , 20,000,000 of people who had a right to claim the influence I , and services of the Church. A policeman has been placed on duty to guard the property doe and night. The spot selected by Gilbert for his strange abode is partially screened, front obser, ation by intervening mounds of earth (rubbish left by barges), and is only reached fitlyr a careful ly- picked walk over marshy ground, and crossing ditches or !rickety plank.. Several fresh discoveries hare been made, I which will have an itnportant bearing on the rase toe police will present to the magistrates at Hammersmith Court this week. Altogether 80 canvas-bags, 40 of, thorn belonging to ths post-office, hare been found, and there is no doubt Got these came into the posse...ion of Gilbert when he was em- ployed at the Brompton ponoffice, prior to hie being pensioner! in 1874. It maty be stated Mr. Flews dispenaes with the use of air pumps and pipes and other similar encumbering parapher. nalia, the means by which he is enabled to effect hie stay under water toeing contained within the diving deem itself. The only connection hetween himself and the surface is a single cord. The principle of the invention consists in purifying the exhaled breath by means of caustic alkali, and revivifying it iigain with oxygen. In thie may the diver breathes the same air over and over again, mines carbonic acid and /A's fresh oxygen at every inspinttion. The means by which this is effect.' consist, in the first place, of a small leather shield, fittest with inlet and outlet valves, and shaped to the contour of the wever'e nose and mouth, over which it in held In position by elastic baud. Over this comes the helmet, which comaela of an inner and outer casing, the sp..c between forming the reservoir for the oxygen, which is there stored under considerable pr saute. The remainder of the apparatus consists 010 couple of puri- fiers, which are slueg one at the back and one in front of the diver, toeing carried benmth the drers. In operation the exhaled breath pongee from the outlet valve in the shield through a lexible tube attached to it and communi- cating with the Irons purifier. Th. consists of a Oat meml- lie chamber, having an inner pertorat.l false bottom, and being divided vertimdly front the top to the false bottom Into two compartments. Each of these compartments con- tain, a mass of indiarobber eponge, saturated with a solu- tion of caustic alkali. The exhaled brmth enters at the top of one compartment, passes down it, through the false bot- tom, and up the second compartment. It then passes through u tube to the purifier ,it the back of the diver,l which is constructed similarly to the front. one. By the time it has ',assist through this second purifier the air has bran deprived ,d all its deleterious abeorptione; but to tit it for reapiration it must he revivified. To this end it enters i the interior of the helmet and mrrounds the diver's head,, where it meets and allndses with a supply of pure oxygen, which is admitted front the more in 31/1311 quantities by the diver as he lisstuires it. The oxygen is stored in the helmet under an Maid pressure of about 2001 b. per square inch,' and its admission into the air space is regulated by means of a small valve worked front the outside of the helmet. The storage space in the helmet is sufficient to cord.tin four cubic feet of oxygen, which supply will last boar booml that being the longest time a diver would be required to re-1 main under water in ordinary- practice. The purifiere are likewise so proportion.' and charge,' :ts to remain active for a similar period. The invention will, no doubt, be found very useful in the numerous eases, which are of daily tx currence, eepecially in connection with docks and similar works, where the services of a diver are required only oc- casionally, but then quickly, when it would prove of con- siderable advantage to be relieved from the presenee of the ordinary paraphernalia and the neeessary attendants. Peter ; anti the Papal representative was also commissionst to olmain at the same time amigo, from other celebrated masters, that he might compare their skill with that of Giotto. Arrived in the city, we are told the courtier .proceeded one morning to the studio where Giotto won at work, and haring informed him of the purpose of his visit and of the manner in which his twister was desirous of mak. tog nee of his services, he a.lost him if he would prepare some design which he could take back with him as a speci- men of his skill. Giotto, it is said, who was on-wry pleasant and courteous man, thereupon bmk a sheet of paper, and, placing his arm firmly loin, side to keep it steady, drew with one stroke of his pencil, which w-as dippsi in., red colour, a circle which WAR so accurate and exact that it was wonderful to see ; and, indetsl, " round.. Giotto's 0 "lot- came eventually a proverb throughout Italy. This com- pleted, he handed it to his visitor, and said, with a smile, " Here is your drawing." "And on, Ito have but this? I asked for a dmign," said the imaged messenger, thinking that Giotto must be jesting. "Go sir," mid the great painter. "I tell you your master needs nothing else from me." At the Royal-Society soiree there wae an instrument of particularly ingeniona construction and of much practi- cal value exhibited—the termiograph, an instrument der signed by Mr. A. M. Rymer-Jonea to plot to an accurate scale the section of the ground over which it travels. The tdottrd sections of the country around Charlton, in Kent, and other places which were exhibited showed the accuracy of its performances. The instrument is as simple as it is Ingenious. The front wheel works the recording gear, the two supporting wheels work an endless roll of roper. As the machine Is pushed over the ground one dire, placed vertically, rotates over another disc which works hori- spinally. If the vertical disc works over the centre of the horizontal one there is a minimum of motion, orals corre- sponding straightness of record, hut no the instrument in working up hill or clown hill it is more or loss inclined, and the vertical di.' slides forwards or backwards And rotates the more rapidly or it travels over the faster-moving areas of the horizontal disc, and the recording ,rear rises from the level proportionately and marks the correfflianding elevations of the section to scale on paper. 30:7-you:axle ERUPTIONS AND EARTIINVAINS.

These will cover the whole of the questions put ho" Beta," MO will no doubt be interesting to some of your readers. whilst entailing but little trouble to me to send you one or more of these sections weekly. Ap?ended is ,eetier I The Legal Requisites of Marriage. The law of England consideta marriage in no other light than as a civil sattract. The holiness of the matrimonial state is left mtirely to the ecclesiadical law. The temporal courts have no jurioliction to mender unlawful tnarriage as a sin. but tnerely as. civil inconvenience. The punishment, therm , fore, or annulling of aced t sous or other nuscriptural marriages, lathe province of the spiritual mods. Tokiag it thus in a civil point of view the law Beata itacit doee all ; other contracts: allowing 11 10 be good and valid in all cases where the parties at the time of making it were, in the firer place, willing to g enact; secondly, able to contract; and , lastly, equallv. did contract, in the proper forme and ! soletunitiel req;ured by law. First, They must be 'ogling to contract. 'Consensus, non concubitue, tacit emotion, is the maxim in the civil law In this CAS,. and it is adopted by !. the common lawyers, whet Indeed have borrowed (especially , in ancient times) almost all their notions of the legithnacy of marriage from the canon and civil laws. Secondly, They , must he able to contract; that is, they must labour under no dkabilitv or incapacity. Thirdly. The parties must not only be willing and able to contract, but must artually teat f themselves in due form of law, to make ha good civil marriage. Any contract made per %Trim de pnesenti, or in ' words of lb.. pt'esent tense', and, in c ise of cohabitation, per ' verbs de futuro also, between persons able to contract, was formerly deemed a valid arnage to many purposes; and . , the parties might be compelled in the spiritual courts to , . celebrate it in focie ecclesite. Put these verbal contracts are ' now of no force, to compel a future marriage. Neither !any ntarriage at present valid, that is not celebrated in come parish church, or public chapel, unless by dispensation from the archbinhop of Canterbury. It must also be preceded by publication of banns, or by license from the spiritual judge. Many other formalities are likewise prescribed by the statutes, the neglect of which, though penal, does not in. validate the marriage. It is hold to he also essential to al 'marriage th.tt it be performed by a person in holy orders, though the intervention of. priest to solemnise this contract in merely jorisimeilivi, and not juris naturalie aut divini. ' But, as the law now stands, orveoynpon the whole that no marriage by the tentnoral law is ipso facto void,that is celebrated by a person in orders,—in a parish church, or Public chapel .(or elsewhere by special dispensation, in pm- mance of banns or ticense, !relateca single persons—consent- ing,—of mond rnind,—and of the age of twenty-one years ; —or 0( 11,0 age of fourteen in moles and twelve in fetishes, with consent of parents or guardians, or without it in case of widowhood. And no marriage is voidable by the ecclesiastictl law after the death of either of He parties; nor during their liven, unless for the canonical impedimenta of pre-Contract (if that indeed still exists), of coneangulnily, and of affinity; or corporal imbecility eubeisting previous to the marriage. We deem it necessary to add, to this general outline, some particulars collected from the several marriage acts which have been panted during thdpresent reign.-1. According to the late act,4 Geo. IV. chap. 76,1 k, into,, must be published in an audible manner in the parish church. or a public chapel belongin, to the parish where the parties reside, upon three Sundays procbding the marriage, during the morning service, immediately after the second lesson ; or the evening service if there be none in the inciting. If the tdrtiee reside in different parishes the banns are lobe published in both. The names places, and time of abode of the parties, must be given to the minister seven days prior to the publication.- 2. By the 5 and 6 Geo. IV., marriages are declared legal which are solemnisol in any other place than the parish church and chapel, to which other place the bishop of the diocese may have granted A liovese for the solentnizafion of marriages.-3. If the marriage be not solemnised within three monthe after the first publication, it is necessary they should be republished. The same period is prescribed in the case of an imended marriage by license.-4. It must alro be sworn that one of the patient bas had his or her usuol place of abode for 15 days immediately preceding the license with- in the parish or chapelry, where the marriage is to be mlemnized. In cam caber of the portion, not being ft widow or widower, is under 21 years, it must be sworn that the con- sent of the person, whom 'consent is requisite, has been obtained. And, if there lio no perann having authority to consent, then upon oath to that effect, by the party requir- ing the license, such license may be granted-5. By special li..ease, or dispensation, from the arbhbishop of Canterbury, marriages may be celebrated at a private house, out of canonical hour, in the evening, or in other parish churches than where one of the parties reeides.-6. The solemnim• lion is prohibited during Lent and on fasting days ; but persons may marry under 'Menne during Lent although the' bands cannot then be published.-7. ............. One hardly needs, I 'impose, to tell your correspondent, "J. Marsh, St. Helens,' that the nightmare is simply an oppression felt on the stomach in sleep. The expression is as old as the hills, and there wets to he no definite knowledge as to how it originated. The northern nations, we are told, called any female dl or ph ntom by the name ..f mare, Ifinschen says, "because they that be troubled with this disease in the night are 30 presse I that they ,'em to haves whole horse laid on them ; or that horses, or chiefly mores, are troubled herewith, that in the morning von shaH find them all in a sweat." Bacon, in his Natural .klistory, says that mushrooms 00050 the incubus, or "the mare in the stomach." Excitement and fear, I fancy, will produce it. I know that when I woes youngster and used to listen till nut hair stood on end to each stories as" The Forty Thieves," "Jack, the Want Killer," du, I was often troubled with the nightmare. J. B. S. 48.—Loans ov Mason.. l-J.M's'' gnestion iffiest week is open to considerable treatment in the way of explanation, aml that without being verbose. One has to take a leap backwards to the customs of our Saxon forefathers to get at the origin of manors and manorial rights which have been preserved through cen- turies. Manor comes front the word rnaneo, signifying to stay. A manor, being the usual residence of the owner, ems the London Encycloprodia, seems to have been a dis- trict of ground held by lord, or great permnages ; who kept in their own hands so much land as was necessary for the use of their families. These rands woe called term domin- Males, or demesne lands ; being occupied by the lord, or donde. imnerii, and his eervants. The other, or tene- mentol lands, they distriliuted anteng their tenant,; which, from the different modes of tenure, were called and dim tinguished by two different names. First, book land, or charter land, which was hell by 3 deed under certain rents and free services, and in effect differed nothing front free soccsge lands ; and hence have arisen most of the freehold tenants who hold of particular manors, and owe suit and service to the mine. The other species was called folk land, s-hick was held by 000e.,aeaaoe in writing, but dis- tributed among the common folk at the pleasure of the lord, aril resumed st his discretion being indeed land held in I viilenage. The residue of the manor, being emelt ivatssl, ; was termed the lord's waste. and nerved for public roads. and I for common of pasture to the lord and his tenants. Manors were formerly called baronies, as they still are lordships; and mole lord or baron was empowered to hold a domestic court, milesi the court heron, for redreming misdemeanors and nuisances within the manor. and for settling disputes of property among the tenants. This court is an inseparable , ingredient of every manor; toed if the number of suitors ' Mould so fail as not to leave sufficient to make a jury or ho-rage. that is, two tenants at the least, the manor itself is lost. In early times the king's greater barons, who had • I large exten, of territory held under the crown, granted out frequently smaller manors to inferior persons to be held of themsel or,; which therefore now continue to be held under a superior lord, who is called in sock cases the lord para. mount over all these manors; and his mignory is frequently termtd an honor, not a manor: especially fit has belonged to an ancient feudal baron, or has been at any time in the hands of the mown. In imitation whereof these inferior lorde began to carve out and grant to others still more emirate estates, lobe held sent themselves, and were no pro- ceeding downwards in intiniton, till the superior lords oliserved that, by this method of subinfeudation. they lost , all their feud il profito of wardship, marriages:and escheats, which fell into the hands of these mesne or middle lords,who I were the immediate euperiors of the terre tenant, or him who occuoied the land : andel. OW the mesne lords themselves were so impoverished thereby.that they were disabled front performing their sereicee to their own superiors. This occasioned, first, that provisim in the thirty-second chapter of Magna Charta, fl Hen. 111.. that no man should either give or sell his land, withoet reserving sufficient to answer the demands of bis lend: and, afterwards the statute of IVestminffier 3, or quia emptores„ IS Edw. I. c. 1. which directs that, upon all sales,or feoffinents of Land, the feoffee should hold the 3101, not of his immediate fenffer, hut of the chief lord of the fee, of whom suck (miter himself held it. But, thme provisions not extending to the king's two I tenants in capita, the like law concerning them is declared I by the statutes of prierogntiva regis, 17 Edw. tie. 6, and of , 34 Edw. c. 15, by which last all subinfeudstions,nrevloue I to the reign of Edward 1,, were ciinfirmed : but all subsequent to that poled were left open to the king's prerng.ttive. Hence it is clear, that all manors existing at this day must have existed as mrly as Edward for it is essential to a manor th,t there be tenants Alio hold of the lord; and, by to opera; ion of these statutes, no tenant in cepele since flee acceesion of that prince, and no tenant of a common lord slum the statute of qui.ll emptore, could create any new tenants to hold of bimsclf.—Cowell, it may .Se rencaffk d, says that in Mews days, • mlnor rather signmes flee aria- Oiction and royalty incorpermi, than the land or site; for a 'nun leas hen's, manor in gross, as the law terms it, Oat is, the right and interest of a court-barov, with the mrquisites thereto [clewing. 3.0.5, Run Corn.

The Major-Ceara, ia the next officer to the lieutenant-general- His chief hominess is to receive orders front the general, or in his ahemoo from the lientenant-general of the day, which he is to dietribute to the brigade-majors, with whom he is to regulate the guards, convoys, detachments, Ac. In a fixed camp he is charged with the foraging, with reconnoitring the ground for it,and posting the escorts. THE PRESIDENCY. A.New York correspond.mt says that General rlymea Grant will be nontinated to succeed Mr. Hayes in the prmi- dential chair, and no to occupy that distinguished net for a third term, hut his election appears now to he very improb- able. The most careful estimates that can be made with the materials available give General Grant only 215 out of the 600 delegates who have been already appointed Inc various matm to aasemble at the ensuing national Republican con- vention. The friends of the other candidates for the nomi- nation muster almut as follows i— For Mr. Blaine, 252 ; Mr. Sherman, 83 Mr. F.dinunds, 31; Mr. Washburne, 13. Ten states with 150 representatives have yet to appoint their delegates. Of these General Grant may find voting in his favour in three southern states, hut he would etill lack TB votes.

THE NATIONAL FINANCE. Mr. Sherman, the American minister of finance, 'making at a banquet given in his honour by the New York Chamber , of Commerce on Tubby, referred M highly congratulatory terms to the material condition of the United States. Re said the country bad entered upon a period of great pros- perity in every department of industry and commerce. It was only the shiplanildlog trade that needed encouragement, as three-fourths of American commerce was at present Con- ducted under foreign flags, and to mwrect this should be the printery object of American statesmen. Mr. Sherman, in conclusion, urged the merchants to do all in their power to further promote the building in America of iron ships, an industry that had made great progress in the United States during the last few veers. THE PAPER TRADE IN GERMANY AND THE PROTEC- -1.1.m•-ts.—The Gennan protectionists are raising VI agiM- Gm for the re-institution of the export duties on rage. It will IR remembered that these duties were abolished by majoritim during the late Custetns discumien in the Reichstag, and since then the export of rags from Germany bas amuined large dionensions. The consequence is that tloe German paper manufacsurers. whose industry employs mme hundred thousand hands, are amble to obtain sufficient raw material for their manufacture. In Austria and in France these duties are still extant, and the German manufacturers complain that their Austrian rivals are in a position to out- grip them in the prices and quality of their paper. T.' AMERICAN IV., Citoe.-1 he latest reports on the condition of the wheat crop in the Western and North- Western State, differ materially from On. made four or five weeks ay. At that time the prospect was that the winter wheat yield the coming season would be enormous; but since then the whole aituation 'IL been changed, and it is now believed that the crop, so far from being abundant, will fall short of even the general average. It is asaerted, in fact, that more than one half of the crop has failed In all the Western States. In Kansas, for instance, the wheat over a large portion of the state haa been almoet entirely des- troyed. lowa reports that the winter planting is an utter failure. sod the spring outlook is far from good. The reports !torn Illinois are fair; in Minna.. nearly OM half the spring wheat has been sown, but the acreage has not increatied. Missouri shows a better condition of affair, than last spring in regard to winter wheat, and ex hibita an acreage increase of nearly 30 per cent. Nebraska has planted 20 per cent. more spring wheat this season than it did last year, and Dakota makes an equally favourable report. Tire next few weeks will probably change these estimates, so far, at treat,., the spring planting is concerned. According to the hest information on tbe subj,ct. however, there is reason to fear that the winter crop will be a short one.—Sor lark Herald.

A deputation of wearers from the north-east district of Lancsehire waited, ON Tuesday afternoon, upon the general 1 committee of the North and *North-east Lancaahire Cotton ; Spinners' and Manufacturers' Association, in Manchester, ; regarding the demand of the wearers for an advance of five per cent. in wages. Two proposition. were submitted tarts ' delegates—one that the masters should fix an early day for the advanee le be made, and that the whole question be re. 'erred to arbitration. The masters declined to enteruin either proposal. but r,stlirm,l their previous declaration— ' viz., that they would seize the first opportunity of an im- provement in trade to advance the wages of the wearers. Wa not only lament with the Protest—aut—Bitbcp deeignate of Liverpool that 'the Devil newt dead," bat wish the mieerable bigotry dirplayed by th, Canon Ryle and other Conforiaing yd N it ,olorm. ing Chrittinn could be interred in the BILM, [OI.OJ • here with the king of the regions of the Let. It is pitiable to witness the petty religious jealousy which has been evoked iu certain quarters by the apromtment of a Roman Catholic Marquis as the glean, repre- sentative in India arid by the choice of Lord lienrotre as Lord Chamberlain. Last week we stated that Canon Etyle and the luvernees Free Preebyteriant were in • state of excessive irritability that a Catholic innead of • Protestant subject should have been oh men to fulfil the functions of a State official. The Dundee Free , Presbytery has tepee reaolved to petition the Queen and Parliament to send the Marquie of Ripon and the • Earl of Kenmare to the right altuut, and to give their , officer, we suppme, to Protestants es bigoted u them selves. The Record is angry over the app. tmeota ; the Liverpool yd Sinith-West Lancashire Pram!, of the Church Mitsionary &inlet) is equally grieved ' and Lord Oranmore and Browne, the prenident el the Protestant Reformation Society, while aduittiug the , Marquis of Ripon to be " • gentleman id aureate courtesy, no honourable man, and • good member," condemns him as unfit for his position bemuse • lof his religious views. Bigots of due elate , are always discovering "rocks ahead," and an it. coo- etant fear that those who happen to differ witi, them in religious untiment will get the upperhycl in the State. Narrow-minded people, with religious pre• judices, need reminding occasionally that tbt day, of Protestant ascendancy in this country are numbered, and that whenever Parliament directs, as did in the oaee of the Irish Church, the English Ipiteopid Church t,, manage its own affair,, no other religious ! body will to permitted by the columon tense and justice of the people to rise up san dominant church in it. stead. Roman Catholic as he it, the Earl of ' Kenmare haa tholen a delicacy and liberality of sentiment that ought to put Proteetant bigots to the ! blush. As Lord Chamberlain, many livings u.. con- tection with the Established Church are in his gift, and he has at the earliest moment announced the ' surrender of all arrangements of an moleamatimel character &nettled to hie office to Earl Sydney, the Lord High Steward. As to the fear of Roman Catholicism agein getting the upperhand in vi- State, this is evidently a thing that is not devoutly wished by Catholics themselves, for they have discovered that their Church can Live and thrive as ammoaf ully when I unyoked as when yoked to the State. Cardinal Newman has just made a declaration of the opinions , of the Cetii lie hierarchy on this point, and it may somewhat tend to allay the excited feeling, of thou who are no much perturbed by the appoixtmente of the Marquis of Ripon and the Earl of lienmare. Speaking at a meeting of the Catholic Union if Great I Britain on the queetion of the Cone, nit. of Great I Britain to the Roman Catholic faith, the CYclinel said that in times put to pray for ths triumph of re- ligion was to petition for the euccess in politica: and civil matters of certain sovereigns, governments, parties, and nations. But these time, had gone. Catholics did not now depend for the ono- cess of their religion upon the patrot &et of eovereigns, and it would not help them much if they gained it. Queen Mary, for netum, did not do mach for them, for the events of her reign had !stamped on the minds of Englishmen "a fear and a hatred" of Catholim, which, at the end of three centuries, was as fresh and new as ever. Thy beet thing which sovereigna, parliaments, municipal:nen, and other political powers could do for them wee to let them alone. Then, again, they no longer uted for miracles—under which category, the Cardi.: im- plied, the wholesale conversion of England would come. Finally, the Cardinal reduced the "cencrete " object of prayers for the acceptance of the Catholic religion by the people of this country to the cm:vendoet of individuals and the removal from the popular timid of prejudice and ignorance as to what Roman Catholicism means.

Kusetrim, thd-ilungartm patriot. has juet made known to the world, what has long been seepected, that Napoleon 111. played with him and the indepen- dence of the Hunger alle in 1859 the part of a diplomatie deceiver. Kowuth him published a work, the title of which in" My Writing* During the Eerie g.ration," and the Budia.Pesth and Vieuta newspnper,. have been publishing long extracts therefrom. The eminent Hum/mien Meen an interesting convereation he had with Prince Napoleon on the 5.h of May, 1h59, and also with the Prince and Louis Napoleon. Ac- companied by Teleki and Kelapka, Kossuth wee resolved by Prince Jerome Bonaparte end sneered that "the Emperor wished Huey/try to avail herself of the opportunity offer d by the impending war to regain her independence, and would ambit her to achieve that end." The Prince a/oared his {GAG,, that the Emperor wit. dmiroue of securing the indepeudente of Hungary, but mein the condition Met it should bra Constitutional Monarchy. Kossuth, delighted at the proposal, twined Prince Jerome that a Constitutiona/ Monarchy was quite cormonant with the wishes f the nation. 'Hungary'. entire poet," he said, ''he. been monarchical. Personally, lame Republican, but. before all elm, a patriot. lota therefore swept the Emperor', stipulation without any reserve, and may hope that my country will do the same" At eleveu o'clock the same evening Kossuth was vent for to the Tenerife, and tot two hours he was closeted with the Emperor ' and Prince Jerome. The Emperor, in opening the convermation, ccci "The Peierie has reported your viewe to me. I vincerely desire that your patriotic wrihee may be fulfilled. I apprehend that you attach two conditions to Hungary's participation in the war one, that I should exten I the scone of amion from the banks of the Po to those of the Danube and Theis, . the other that I ehould aemmpany the appearance of • my troop, upon Hunwarian nod with a proclamation in which I should make appeal to Hungary's dreieion of 1849, and call upon your nation, as ite friend and ally, to realise its declaration of independenoe, and beech, up arum for the conqumt of our common foe. There is DO virtue m valuable in a young man as thrift, and if lie listens to the voice of the gambling eyren, it is ten chances to one that he will ever have. sovereign in his pocket which he can call his own. Ihe letter has caused quite a flutter in the dove- cote frequentwl hy the class of young men referred to and I heard done elating that he was present when the scene pictured by your correspondent took place—n high compli- ment to his descriptive powers. A student of the philosophy of clothes, like leotol,lntrocluh in it sartor haa only to look carefully at the dress of mme of the lovers of gambling in the town in order to see that even in cams where it is known the young man bass natural love of neat- ness, in every line of his threadbare coat the story is told that Ire is suffering pecuniarily from his devotion to the lamina. ling thing. I cannot lift the veil which bides from view the quarrels mused in mane homes through the almost idiotic conduct of husband., who are earning good wages, spending nearly every surplus shilling in games of chance. I sorely pity Some of these, who are men with talents far above the average, but are year in and year out quietly sinking all their surplus cash in a sea which is almost bottomless. The mental blindness of theee disciples of the god of chance is pitiful to any one who is not swallowed up by the absorbing lexinotirro of the varioue genies, for they appear to think that gentlemen in a higher Is-winOn than themmlves, who could give them help which would enable them to materially advance their position in life, are utterly ignorant as to their proceedings, whereas they are very fairly posited tin lie matter and this very fact hoe caused them to lose all confidence in them. That this is a wise decision no one who has watched the careers of gambler. can for a moment doubt, for who can tell where a man will stop who is once under the fmcination of the evil habit. The advice of friends, the fear of losing the respect of good , men, the love of home, the affection of some fair being, are ' all found too weak to restrain the gambler, who rushes on his headlong course until, possibly, lie is tempted to use the money of an employer, and tied, himself charged with an often. against the law. A ehort time ago I heard of a certain association of men in a neighbouring town to Run- corn which is in far from a prosperoun condition, bemuse its manager. will not permit those who frequent it to gambles I hope that the ventilation of this subject will caum those who are to blame for the state of things referred to by your correspondent to mend their ways. A reader of °Flamm " complains th.tt, though living not far from the Parish Church of Farnworth, he has not heard the sound of the sweet bells for four or five weeks, and, being a musiml mul, he is very touch grieved at the stifle.; which has characterised the tower of the edifice of late. I am told that tide state of things is owing to the church. wardens being so afflicted by poverty—poor mots—that than cannot afford to pay the ringers. Some years ago collections were only made at the church about six times in the year, hut now they are characterised by as great regularity as the rent day and the question arises of how it is that the church-wardens are left in such a poverty stricken con- dition.

So far as I can learn those clever fellows out in India have not found the four million sovereigns I mentioned last week as missing. 1 tell you that a million would need some vending, as it means fifteen mike of sovereigns laid flat, edge to edge; but four millions, oh, iee a poser ! A sum like that cannot be eaten before breakfast, crammed into a corner, or lost in the nook of a vest pocket. Look here! You know what the thicknese of a .C 5 Bank of England note is. Well, I've no doubt you think you could cram a million like those into your hat, and still find room in the tile for your head. You are under a elight misapprehension. A million note, piled one on the top of the other would reach a height 01 416 feet, and four millions of them would extend 1,644 feet, or make up a monument of 5,54 yards and 2 feet. Itoot you think those Indian fellows might see a pile like that without an eye glen.? As they haven't seen anything of the kind wandering about without an owner, let us see what the appearance would be if a million notes were spread about. Why they would cover a space of 250,000 feet. And still they have not been seen ! How the money has gone without somebody knowing that it had gone until ten days after its disappearance would matte , Cocker himself. If the fellow who kept the key of the each box had been playing at" chuck penny" with eovereigns, and he threw • hundred sovereigns a minote for ten hours every day, it would take hint nearly 68 days to pitch all the lour millions away. You eee an egg ant butterman has found that out, thousands upon thimainds of miles distant from where the money is missing. In the name of Cocker, then, where is the "brass ?"

Mr. BENJAMIN BROWN moved that the Board ehould accede to the prayer of What he might call the memorial, and , Hat they should in future decline to let the land which had , formed)/ been need for the porpoise of holding the fair. He was of ophion that it was the duty of the members to sup- port a memorial which canoe hewn each a baly of influential gentlemen as those constituting the Widnes School B.ht. fie eaw that the amount which the Board obtained for the letting of the land was £29, but he was eure that this repre- sented Whet was really a very great loss to the neighbour- hood. Ile did not believe there wee a shopkeeper in Anne- street or Victoria-roed hut would be willing, if necessary, to subscribe his quota towards the raising of mach a sum rather than have the fair continued. He could quite endorse the representation Ott& Or to the immoral influence which the thing complained of exerciatak. Ile might .ay that he had the pleasure of rneetieg 31r. Carey on the ground during the progress of the fair. (Laughter.) Well, he did not really know whether it reuse pleasure or not. In mmcluding his observations upon the It-latter he on& say that he was quite aure the remarks contained in the cmnmunication that had been received were not made without very good cause. Mr. BANEIIRRS7 begged to second the motion. Mr. Cense moved an amendment 00 1110 effect that the subject stmuld be referted to the Markets Committee for consideration. Having understood that this half-yearly fair was objected to by a good many persons, he had, at the re- coat githering held upon the ground opposite, renewed the marlines he had previemely made; and on Saturday week he and Mr. lituspratt visited the fair together. He dare.), that they spent on hour and a half there, going into several of the booths—(laughter)—and in and out, gathering all the information tlegy could. He must coy he Woe surprised I to find how —llttle drunkenness there wae. In foot, lie only saw one glrunken man there, and he was such i an individu"al that he believed he would have been drunk , wherever for load been. (Laughter.) The fair was crowded , with working people of the neighbourhood, amoaget Wilolll he caw a great many of the most temperate and Seedy in the town. He hod the pleasure of meeting Mr. Brown mid Mr. Dickson there and, es far as he could gather, there WAr I nothing going on to which the Board could resraorably object. He would not recapitulate the argument, he had considered on previous ORCORMIS in favour of and against the holding of the fair. Ile might say that he saw the Inspector of polio° there, and he asked him whether, in his opinion, there was any increase of drunkennees cane.] by the holding of the fair, and he gave utterance to an opinion which he had expresseal on mother occasion, to the effect that there was no increase, but, if anything, there were rather fewer eases of drunkenness at the fair time than on other occasions. He (the speaker) had come to the conclusions that the fair, although it woe a rough Pant of entertainment, and not the kind of one which they, as tnembers of the Local Board, would all pope, yet del not necessarily include anything of a prejudicial character. Mr. Bannow, in eeconding the amendment, said he endorsed the remark. made by Mr. Carey, and he might even say lie could even go a little further and state that if the inembere of the School Board would only notice what a falling-off there would be in the attendance at the school, during IVhil week, and the manner in which many of the people would enjoy themselves, they would come to the conclusion that the two compared very badly with what occurred on the ground opposite during the fair week. Ile was quite of Mr. Corey's opinion, that it was better to have the hOOBIS concentretel on the piece of open ground opposite the Board offices, and under a supervision which must naturally prevent crime and drunkenness tee large extent. He visited the fair-ground on the Saturday night, but only fore hew minutes, and the great bulk of these enjoying it were children. What were the children to do or, a Satur- day aft,noon when there was no school? It was certainly far better to hove the children or others concentrated on the open groitrot opposite the Board-room than to have them amusing themselves by breaking windows in empty cottagee and other games of that sort. Everybody who had thought upon this subject must have come to the conclusion that such enjevments es those to be had at a fair time must be presided for the manes of the people. He did not like this principle of attempting to put everybody on one platform, for all were not lovers of tea meetings and tbinge of that sort. Personally, he adminal tea meetings, penny readings, , and other attempts to find pleasant recreation for the work- ing classes, but it was not right to try to prevent other , people having their little enjoyments. He eincerely hoped ! that the communication which had been received would be referred to the committre for consideration. Mr. flitoww, in reply, said Mr. Carey had stated that he did not see any drunken people at the fair. Well, all be could say as to that wee that he did not think Mr. Carry 1. went to the right place to look for them. Then must not forget that people were not allowed to sell Leer on the fair round. He k the speeker) must aty that when he visitol the fair he saw a good deal of drunken men at the hotele surrounding the land on which it was held. Certainly it wan true that An. the Local Board had taken the matter in hand the booths had been more concentrated in one place. Title, he suppesed, was oveing to the Board having made it their business to take the fair under their wisg, and thus they had attracted many of the most respect- able portion of the community to the place where it was held. But they did not want any more of this sort of thing. (Hear, hear.) The seconder of the amendment had said something about being agreeable to tea meetinge being held, hut it war not.. question as to what Mr. Barrow was agree- able to, but what that Board was doing. What he wished was that the members would treat the fair in the same manner as they did other thing', and let it Alone. 'Pile amendment was then put and carried, seven members voting for it. It was next put as a substantive motion, .d carried with only one dissentient—Mr. Brown. OAR AND WATER COMMITTEE.

A Hit:olol,2BM FRT.:imam/arc POIL LivISIIPOOL.— We publiali to-thy tbe prospectua of the International Marine Hydropathic Co., which has been formed by a number of influential residents of Liverpool and the neighbourhood for the purchase of the mansion and grounds known as Scofield, at Waterloo-with-Seaturth, on the estuary of the Mersey. Hitherto there toe been no hydropathic esfiblishment in the vicinity of Liverpool, and the new undertaking commences under very favourable circumstances, both as to the terms of purchase and the character .of the property to be acquired. The mansion (which wee built for a private residence) is handsome and large, and the grounds comprise about nine acres of freehold land, with most capacious glom housea,l which will require but slight adaptation for the use and recreation of visitors in all weathers. In his treatise on land- scape gardening, published a few years ago, Mr. Edward Kemp gives a detailed account of the glum hon.. at Sea- field (then in course of erection), and observee Alto- nether, when completed, this magnificent series of glass booms will be among the most perfect, unique, and COM- pact examples of the kind in the country, for everything is being carried out in the most liberal spirit. and with the best modern appliances." The property has been visited by most of the inetlical profession in the locality, and they have unanimously expressed their opinion that "the situation and the premises are well suited for the proposed establish- ment." It is well-known that American and Canadian tra- vellers have long felt the want of a first-class establishment where, on their arrival in Liverpool with their families they can find quiet together with the comforts they are emus- • towed to in their own well-appointol hotels. The com- pally will thus supply a want hitherto uoprovided for from evely point of view. The undertaking is being inaugurated with the prospect of great success. The whole of the ordi- • nary shaves have been applied for, and the subscription list for the six per rent.'preference capital opens to-day. div.head: CONEREGATIONAL UNION.
div.p: THE CONEREGATIONAL UNION.

The manual meeting of the Congregational Cnion of England and Wales watt opened on Monday night in the Memorial Hall, London, Professor Newth presiding. The annual report, which was adopted, stated that the special committee appointed to consider the reform in the college system had reported in favour of the establishment of educa- tional boards to further college work, and elimulate intermt in minieterial education. The report also expressed the belief that questions affecting relieions equality would receive more just consideration in the preseat Parliament than in any previous Parliament ninon the Commonwealth. Dr. Alton was elected chairman for the ensuing year, and several alterations having been made in the standing orders, the conference adjourned. lahe meeting was resumed on Tuesday morning in West- ininster Chapel, the Rev. for. broth, the chairman far the year, presiding, supported by Mr. H. Richard, M.P., Mr. H. Lee, M.P., Dr. Mellor, Rev. J. G. Roger,, and others. After the usual devotional service, the rev. Chairman delivered hie inaugural address, in which he dwelt at length upon the ' Nation and prospects of Congregationalism and its place among the Churches of the world. On the motion of the Rev. A. Hannay, s reference committee was appointed, to whom was referred the question of passing come resolution to strengthen the bands of Mr. H. Richard, M.P., in his endmvour to bring ebout mutual diartmament. The Her, E. WF,SLEYAN DISTRICT MEETING AT WARRINGTON. ' PUBLIC TEMPERANCE MEETING. The first public meeting ilk connection with the Liverpool i district aeries was held or 110,m.y-road Chapel, Warrington, on Monday erening. Hey. W. T. Radcliffe occupied the I chair. There were elm on the platform the Revs. C.tiorratt, J W Berry, R. F. Cape, T. T. Lambert, and U. Walker. After prayer, the (711,11.1.Ve said there were many signe of progress in the movement they had met to advocate. In Ireland then had get Sunday closing, and the returns of the excise for the eel ea showed that there had been less drink consumed. Perhaps that might he accounted for by bad times, but he • looped that it might be by the increased wisdom of the peoplo. The great political changes that had occurred held eat to them great hopes of. future reformation. Titer were reward In a plan that united moral means, but Alit they did nio object to swim legislation to help Ahem. For himself, be saw no inwadon of the liberties of the people by the Local Optiott Bill. The nation was ruled by o majority, asid he did not see Isla, a district should cot be. The per- missive legislation bad not done much good of late, yet the Permisnive Bill was worthy of mock consideratiou. He hoped that soon the Chaocellor of the Each; quer might have to get his reventie froin another source than froin the drink traffic—(hear, heart—nod that hit budget would be entirely revolutionised Them was great hope of future success for their movement. (Cheere.) The Rev. J. R. Reser rejoiced in the improved cmdition of the temperance movement. One of the great hindrances to the Church of Christ of that day meethe groe log intem- perance of the land. There MIS great hopes in store for them, and let them all try to lessen the great misery and wretchedness that prevailed in the laud through that abominable traffic by doing all they could to push forward the temperance movement. (Applause.) The Rev. T. T. latungor said that in order that they might not underestimate the treinendous amount of worit that would be required ere they conquered the drink traffic, he would give them a few statistics of the strength of the enemy. In the United Kingdom, there were 195,000 public housen, awl in liquors there was spent per year,1142,000,000 or between 5.1 and Li per head of every living person in England. Gist year there were 175,000 persona on the poor law bent, of the diffierent unions in England, and fivessisthis of (ho psuperiam could he traced directly to drink. It was AA antis' fact that England, posseseing one fourth of the entire trade of the globe, there ehould be one eleventh of the whole impulation who never got through a aingle year with- out going on the rates. 100,000 people were annually con- victed before the magistrates, of course, through drink, elm 300,000 vagranta t and during the last 90 yeare the lunacy of the country had doubled itself. One of the highent Mieutific medical authoritieis in the kingdom mid that if, by any miracle England could be converted Be adorn, from intoxicating drinks, the vitality of the people would rise one third. He advised total abstinence, because of example, moral 'melon in reference to the drunkard, nerd legislative probibiton in reference to the traffic. (Ap- PL10.0.1 The Iter. Counter GA 11, on rking to speak was greeted With loud applause. He said it seemed to hint a very lilting thing that their first meeting of an official character should be held In Warrington. He was extremely glad that it was Iseld at Warrington that year, becaum it was a remarkable year in the history of temperance. Fifty years ago at that very time the first attempt at anything liken temperance organimtion was being made at Warrington. To War- rongton belonged the high honour of being the second place that made any attempt at temperance organization, Bradford began it. Warring-too seconded it and then it imrang across to Manchester aud Liverpool, and then to l'reston where by the interference of the holy spirit Joseph Liveser took hold of it, and by the Kuidance of hie wise head ao,l brave heart it reached the eminence that they saw it at that day. (Cheers 1 Ile might ooy—
Small and feeble was t Ike day, Whey. Ile first the work bevin."

The work came out of the Church, and the world seemed to be trying tomb the Church of her honours. They hall to look back and see in that beneficial movement an illustration of the gmeroue utterances of the Jews,“howbeit God turned the curse intro blessing." The temperance movement sprang out of the dimppointat hopes of a minister—the noble Gr. Lyman Beecher. (Cheers ) The temperance movement io the Church had been through the ordinary 'Konen. that every good movement had to undergo. Rest it was denounced, next it was tolerated, and finally it was willed upon, adopted, and became an essential of the Ghttrch. Other men hail laboured, nnd they had retired into their labours. It watt special organization for meeting a special necessity. It wagon evil no tongue could describe, and no pen could be any possibility portray. The net election bad sounded the death knell id the drink traffic. (Cheers.) Manufacturers had had notice to quit. (Laugh- ter.) They had taught them that the men who were the great promoters of the violation of the laws ought not lobe legislators, and they had taught then) that men who showed their drat consideration for their trade and not the interest of the counny were traitors, and ought not to be in their legis- lature —)cheers)—and so they have got notice to quit even la the three jolly Allsopps. (Cheers.) They bad now a Parliament prepared to listen to the voice of the people— hear, kneel—if the people were prepared to speak on the übject. The responsibility would remain on the people and not on the legislators now. If they were apathetic they would remain if they were in earnest they bad a glorious time before them. The Chancellor of the Encheqbhor might have some difficulty people said to make up the revenue, but when he remembered that their police anti 11 001. rate last rear am dounted to no lest than fifteen an a half millions, he k'nerri that if the drink traffic was annihilated 1 millions would be sufficient, and then the Chancellor of the Exchequer would he compensated for all loss that he might sustain through the non-arrival of the drink revenue. (lime, bear.) One of th'e things he never could forgive the late Government wae the granting of longer hours for drinking. (near, hear.) They mutt go in shortening the hour% and give the landlords a walk before breakfast. (Cheers.) They must go in for the entire suppression of beerhomes—(hear, hear)—and the closing of public-houses on a Monthly. (Cheers.) He held a strong opinion upon that. It was not the work of the teetotaller ; it was the work of the Church. Iltrar, hear.) If they believed the Church lobe a di Mile ordination. then the opening of public-housea on a Sunday was a national sin. That Wall a lime when England expected every man to do his duty. If public-houses were not chased an Sundays it would not he his fault. Let every man resolve to do the some. and they would be accomplished. (Hear, hear.) He should like to ate the new Parliament deluged with petitions on the matter,. that when the business of the new Parliament tommenced every member—including their honoured member, Mr.McMinnies !cheers, might present a petition on that question. The reverend goutlenGn then spoke about the good being done bveneoa house% and con- cluded with an appeal for increased svinpathy in the temperance movement. (Applause.) The Rev. R. Cape said that after such a filch from their " Prime :Minister," he need not say much. Hc alluded briefly to the conversion of the newspaper press in the great matter of temperance. If c was glad to see that the greatest organ for the reformation of the world—the printing press—was doing its duty on that subject, and encouraging It in every way. The newspaper leaders used to carimture the teetotallers in every possible way. A temperance meet- ing furnished food for an excellent joke in which the ministere who took part were described as eo many "Rev. Siigginee or Chathands, with suspiciously red noses, who looked as though they liked a steaming bowl of hot punch —on the sly." Their facetious friend, Mr. P.. neh, bad woven graceful chard.. to Adorn the brow of temperance. , In a few verses awhile age, he (Pooch( proclaimed what they tedotallers hall been proclaiming, viz., that total abstinence from intoxicating drinks provided hoalth and long life. The Rev. E. J. 'Tnewts, of Liverpool, addreased the meeting and spoke principally upon the importance of inculcating the principles of obedience to parents in rho minds of the young. Those who were parents were sensible of the difficulty of teaching and training their children, and those who were not parents hoptnl to bt coin° so, and therefore ought to lay inn stock of ability re tcly to do the teaching when the time , arrived. They 1,.1,1 sometimes beard the question mired that was raised long, long ago," what manner of child shall thishe." Most mothers had nondered;wben they looked °pan their lathe., how they would turn out, what surfer parents, if spared to grow up they would be. The sense of the import. ance of character was a growing ono, and that was the ad. trance of civilizatitm, and the Christ ialiity that characterised the world, there tens greater sense " character than us,d

of the importance of to be cherished. But they were never likely to hope the best concerning their children. Here and them phrenologists fold them that there were instances of persons who had not hope go very largely developed ; indeed below the overage. That was not • comfortable state of !existence, but, perhaps a great many persons hoped troll for their children. Ile did not know whether all persons who were parents thought that the first lesson they neoled to teach their children was that of obedience. It was raid that John Locke, the philooopher, was once spoken to be a lady, who requested that he would lae good enough to give her some rule for the treatment of her boy. "Hoer old in be," John Locke asked, "Three years." she mid. Ob." said he, "It is too late." Most persons would think he was Joking, but most of them thought that solo< sort of discipline needed to be exercised upon a child rather early, and the , very lira lesson to be taught was that of obedience. If they did not get their children to know that thew must obey their parent., under what circumstances would they be led ! to obey Almighty God whom they did not see. Thom who were proprietors of schools, ermeciallvboarding schools,were often somewhat troubled by the different claws of tempers in their mtablishments. It did not seem quite fair that thrice who were parents should just /Mirk their chief doty to their children and let it go to the care of others, who generally had the thankless task of subduing their will. It seemed to him that that might be dorm at home, where the sense of superiority should be imposed upon them, and that was the place where some conegiousnesn of obligation to obey should be arrived at whilst they were young. John Ashworth spoke et having visited establishments for boys, and reformatories for girls, and Ire was told by the matrons of those reformatories that ball man ;ge- ment at home was almost Invariably the eartm of the children being there. And when speaking to governors of training ships the conduct of the boys was attributed very largely to bad mothers. But it was found that by a few years management of those boys and girls, they were brought into what was called "good form," and left the establiehments, having created for themoelves excellent characters. If that kind of thing could be done for horn and girls by strang,ers, one would think it might be done and ought lobe done by parents. This could be done. D. WOLF, in moving the previous question, contended that the course propoeed was inconvenient, unprecedented, and ir- regular. It wan laid down by Sir Ers`:ine May that the basinese of the House could not he proceeded with until the Speech from the Throne had been read, or until a bill had been read. It was said that the case of Baron Rothschild, which was dealt with by resolution, was relied on. But the question before the HOUB4 was not confined to the case of the member for Northampton. The resolution dealt with the whole question, and it was proposed that the coinmittee should sit even during the adjournment of the Hous,.. He admitted that the Baron Rothschild resolution was panaed before the Queen's Speech had been read, but that was done in con- fornaity with an Act of Parliament which enabled the House by resolution to vary the oath in the case of the admission of a Jew.—The ATTORNEI-Ii.ERAL would not contest the point that in relation to all general matters it wee incumbent on the House not to enter on the business before the reading of the Queen's Speech, but this was a malts r relating to .the swearing of members which formed part of a message from the Throne. With regard to the allegation of undue haste, he maintained that all that was Nought for woe to accent due justioe to the member for Northampton, and he hoped the House would not refuse this act of juntice.—Mr. Luton-row seconded the amendment. Ile said the whole thing was e farce which had been arranged six weeks ago by Mr. Adorn. now First Commiesioner of Works, who wrote down to Northampton imploring the electors to vote for Mr. Brad- laugh, and the prompter throughout had been the Prime Minister.—Mr, Sergeant Simon, The Speaker, Mr. Leighton, Sir R. Knightley, Sir J. Hunter, Mr. GOON, and Sir J. R. Mowbray having spoken, the SOLICIBOR.GINEREL (Mr. Herschell) pointed out that when this committee nor first moved for Sir 8. GOFER° said it meet be distinctly understood that, whatever the decision of the comtnitlee might he, the ultimate decision must rest with the House itself.—Mr. O'DONNELL said that if an hon. mem- ber refused to take the oath of allegiance he ought to state his reasone, and the House in tine cam, ought to know more fully what the facts of the cart were than they had vet been informed by the Government. Ile did not think Mn. Brad' tough hinted' would object to give bin reasons, but it dhl not appear convenient for the Government to state what those moons were. Mr. Bradlaugh had deecribed religion as a disease of the brain, and conscience as • nervous extraction of the diaphragm. (laughter.) They ought not to he in a hurry in the appointment of a committee, for even the hon. member for Bristol. who with high pontifical authority— Gaughterl—at first gave his support to Mr. Bradlaugh, had since add he acted in haste. (Renewed laughterb—The House divided, when the numbers were :—For the previous queetion, 74 against, 171. Majority, 97. The motion that the committee OPERLE of 19 members was then agreed to, an were also the names and leave was given to sit during the adjournment of the House.—The House adjourned at 20 minute. past Bil o'clock until Thursday, May 20. ~.• ...• •

Some people are in luck. There is no owner for Parr Moss—at all events no person has laid claim to it, I under- stand, fur none consilerable tline—and no the residents, or a portion of them, have seized upon the opportunity as a favoivable one to become possessed of a patch of land.' "Why pay root" is the axiom on which they are inclined I to act, that is if no one steps in to prevent theta, and to carry out the laudable intention in view they have been busy of late in coolly selling out the land—some 30 acres, I believe—in quite a friendly and sum- mary manner, as agreed upon between themselves. This in business with a vengeance, and it is only natural that residents in other parts of the borough Cegin to be jmlous of the good fortune of the people of Parr which, however, having tunic under the notice of the authorities, will very likely it nipped in the had. This is tire ~o,"tes operandi which the people of Parr think is all that is re- quired to become a landowner—to partition or not out the load seined upon in lots, to fin poles in the ground, then to write thee- mines on them, and beigh, presto! they are landed proprietors.
